name: PT Bank Maybank Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: A capital-rich, return-poor subsidiary priced for a franchise it does not earn
frontmatter.summary: Maybank Indonesia earns a return on equity far below its cost of equity, yet trades at a premium to book that assumes a recovery we cannot source. Loans are growing again and costs are controlled, but the margin is thin, the credit print is flattered by a strong fourth quarter, and a free-float deadline hangs over the register. We initiate at REDUCE.
thesis: The franchise earns a fraction of its cost of equity; on warranted P/BV the shares are worth about three tenths of book, not the premium the market pays.
The FY2025 profit jump leans on an unusually strong fourth quarter; the nine-month run-rate points to lower earnings in FY2026 even with loans growing again.
Capital is not the constraint — the capital ratio is among the highest in the sector — so the value case rests entirely on lifting returns, which the cost and margin trends do not yet show.
{'The register is the second problem': 'the controlling shareholder must lift the public float to the exchange minimum, an overhang rather than a catalyst.'}
Our twelve-month target sits well below the traded price; the house regime lens closes only part of that gap within the year, so the rating stays negative rather than outright short.

catalysts.event: FY2026 full-year results and the dividend declaration
Exchange deadline for the first step of the free-float requirement
Close of the index provider's consultation on Indonesia's market status
Index provider decision on Indonesia's classification

blocks.text: We initiate on Bank Maybank Indonesia at **REDUCE** with a twelve-month target of **Rp130**, **-16.2%** against the traded price of **Rp163**. The target is not the fundamental value. On a probability-weighted blend of residual income, warranted P/BV and dividend discount the equity is worth **Rp86** per share, and our konglo lens — which assumes only part of today's premium decays inside a year — lifts the twelve-month number to the target. The distinction matters for how the call should be read. The shares are expensive because the business earns a low return on equity against a high cost of equity, not because the bank is about to fail. It is over-capitalised, adequately provisioned and funded by a parent with a long record in the market [S14].

Three things move the value. First, the return on equity: our forecast path sits near **4.1%** against a cost of equity of **12.5%**, and nothing in the recent results suggests that gap closes quickly [S14][S2]. Second, credit: the price sits above every one of our valuation methods, so it is not a modestly better credit outlook that closes the gap but a return on equity the bank has never sustained [S14]. Third, the register: the controlling shareholder holds a stake that leaves the public float below the exchange's minimum, and the first compliance step falls due on 31 March 2027 [S17].

The bull case is honest and we state it below: loan growth has turned positive, the cost of funds is improving as cheap deposits grow, and a parent that has already injected capital once could simplify the group structure in a way that crystallises value [S2][S6]. We do not think that is the most likely path within twelve months, and the price already pays for a good deal of it.

Bank Maybank Indonesia is a mid-sized commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by Malayan Banking Berhad, which reports the bank as a subsidiary of the Maybank group [S14]. The annual report sets out a shareholder composition in which two Maybank group vehicles hold the large majority of the shares, with a small strategic holder and a public tranche making up the balance [S14]. Operationally the bank runs two businesses: Community Financial Services, which covers retail, small and medium enterprise, micro and business banking, and Global Banking, which covers corporate lending, treasury, global markets and transaction banking [S14]. A sharia business unit sits alongside the conventional bank and contributes a material slice of group revenue through margin income that the consolidated accounts report inside net interest income [S14].

The balance sheet at the end of FY2025 was **IDR193,720.0bn** of assets, **IDR123,640.0bn** of gross loans and **IDR116,190.0bn** of customer deposits [S13][S14]. The loan book is skewed to corporate and commercial exposures, with consumer mortgages and motorcycle financing through the group's multifinance arm filling out the retail side; Community Financial Services alone held **IDR87,170.0bn** of loans [S14]. Funding is deposit-led, with a meaningful current-account and savings component that management put at **IDR79,810.0bn** of cheap deposits and a CASA ratio of **64.1%** by the third quarter, up from **57.6%** at the previous year-end [S10]. That mix is the heart of the franchise argument: cheap deposits are the only durable source of margin for a bank of this size, and the CASA build is the single most positive operating development of the past year [S10][S2].

Strategy is framed in the annual report as the ROAR programme, a five-year plan running from FY2026 that replaces the earlier transformation plan and targets customer experience, community impact and sustainable growth rather than a stated financial destination [S14]. The plan's concrete elements are the ones we can test: selective lending growth in corporate and SME, digitisation of the transaction stack, and cost discipline through a programme the bank calls SCMP [S14]. The structure goes the other way round: at an extraordinary general meeting on 29 June 2026 the shareholders approved Bank Maybank Indonesia itself becoming the *Perusahaan Induk Konglomerasi Keuangan* (PIKK) for the Maybank financial conglomerate under OJK Regulation 30/2024, taking over shares in Maybank Sekuritas Indonesia, Maybank Asset Management, Asuransi Etiqa Internasional Indonesia, Maybank Indonesia Finance and WOM Finance [S6]. Two of those are already consolidated subsidiaries — Maybank Indonesia Finance at almost the whole equity and WOM Finance at a majority stake — so the transfer adds the securities, asset-management and insurance legs to the listed bank rather than moving the bank under a new holding company [S14][S6]. The announcement gives no consideration, no share issuance and no completion date, and we could not source either; we therefore treat the transfer as an intra-group reorganisation at fair value, with assets received matched by cash or shares given, which leaves value per share unchanged but makes the share count and the funding of the consideration the two things to watch [S6].

Competitively the bank is a challenger, not a leader. It sits in the third capital tier by size, well below the state-owned banks and the largest private groups, and its share of system loans is small in absolute terms [S14][S15]. The branch footprint is national but concentrated in Java and the major cities, and the brand rides on the parent's regional franchise rather than on a distinct domestic identity [S14]. That position explains both the strategic logic — leverage the group's corporate relationships and its technology — and the financial problem, which is that a sub-scale bank with a corporate-heavy book earns a structurally thinner margin than the leaders [S14].

A bank of this kind typically lives or dies on three things: the spread between what it pays depositors and what it earns on loans, the credit losses it takes on the lending book, and the operating cost of running branches and systems. Scale helps all three, because large banks fund themselves more cheaply, diversify credit risk across more borrowers and spread fixed costs over more revenue. When a mid-sized bank is owned by a larger regional group, the group can supply funding, technology and cross-border corporate business, but it can also constrain the local franchise to the role of a supporting node.

The Indonesian banking system is growing faster than the economy. Credit across the industry rose by double digits in the year to September 2026, with the regulator reporting loan growth in the low-to-mid teens and deposit growth around a high single-digit rate for the period, corporate lending leading while household credit lagged [S15]. That is a strong backdrop for any lender with capital to deploy, and it is the main reason the loan book here has turned from contraction to growth, with gross loans at **IDR128,390.0bn** by September against **IDR123,640.0bn** at the prior year-end [S3][S10]. The policy rate has been stable, which anchors funding costs and gives banks room to compete on the asset side without a sharp repricing of deposits [S5].

Competition is intense and stratified. The state-owned banks dominate corporate and payroll lending, the large private banks dominate cards, wealth and mass-affluent deposits, and the digital challengers are taking share in unsecured retail at prices that make sense only for a lender with a low cost base [S15]. Mid-sized banks such as this one compete on relationship lending to corporates that value speed and on SME lending that the largest banks find too small to serve profitably [S14]. The result is a market where the leaders earn a return on equity comfortably above their cost of capital and the middle of the pack struggles to cover it, which is exactly the pattern our numbers show [S14].

On the five-forces view, supplier power sits with depositors and is rising as savings products proliferate; buyer power sits with large corporate borrowers who can price the banks against each other; the threat of new entry is real in digital retail but not in corporate lending, where relationships and balance-sheet capacity are barriers; substitution comes from capital markets and fintech credit; and rivalry is high and worsening as loan growth outpaces deposit growth across the system [S15]. The bank's moat is therefore narrow: the parent's brand and the corporate relationships it brings, the sharia franchise, and a cheap-deposit base that is improving but still smaller than the leaders' [S10][S14].

Regulation shapes the industry more than any commercial factor. The regulator sets capital, liquidity and provisioning rules, requires quarterly public financial disclosures, and the exchange has been tightening transparency and free-float requirements for listed companies [S17]. The exchange now publishes a list of companies with high shareholding concentration and has removed those names from its headline index calculation, a disclosure regime that directly affects this stock [S8]. Alongside it, the index provider's consultation on Indonesia's market classification has frozen index increases for Indonesian names, which removes a source of passive demand that mid-cap banks previously counted on [S19].

The practical consequence for this bank is that its cost of equity should not be flattered by index inclusion. A stock that is out of the headline index, with a public float of **11.2%** against a regulatory minimum, faces a narrower investor base and a higher required return than a comparable bank with a broad register [S8][S17]. That is not a moral judgment about the controlling shareholder; it is a mechanical input into the discount rate, and we treat it as such in the valuation below.

The industry's own growth is also the risk to the industry. Deposit growth lagging loan growth means funding competition will decide margins over the next year, and a bank that must pay up for deposits in order to keep growing is a bank that gives back in margin what it wins in volume [S15]. For a franchise with a thin margin and a high loan-to-deposit ratio on customer funds, that trade-off is the central commercial question, more important than the level of industry credit growth itself [S14].

Banking systems in emerging markets tend to grow loans at a multiple of nominal output while the economy is formalising, and to consolidate slowly around the largest institutions as capital and technology requirements rise. Mid-sized banks are squeezed from both ends: they cannot match the funding costs of the largest deposit franchises, and they cannot match the speed of the digital challengers. Those that survive do so by owning a niche — a corporate client base, a diaspora franchise, a sharia franchise — and by keeping operating costs per customer low relative to the revenue each customer generates.

The five-year record is one of a bank that shrank its balance sheet and then stabilised. Gross loans reached **IDR123,640.0bn** at the end of FY2025 after a contraction in the corporate book, while customer deposits slipped to **IDR116,190.0bn** over the same period [S13]. That combination lifted the reported loan-to-deposit ratio and put pressure on the funding side, which management answered by shifting the mix toward cheap deposits rather than by chasing volume [S10]. The result was a year in which profit rose sharply even as the balance sheet shrank, because the fall in funding cost and in provisions did more for earnings than the lost volume did [S13].

Profitability is thin and improving only slowly. Net interest income on the bank's own definition was **IDR7,221.9bn** in FY2025, other operating income **IDR2,326.8bn**, pre-provision operating profit **IDR3,100.0bn**, and pre-tax profit **IDR2,222.8bn** [S14]. The company-reported return on equity was **5.5%**, the cost-to-income ratio **68.5%** and the net interest margin **4.3%** — a franchise that earns its keep but not its cost of capital [S14]. Gross non-performing loans were **2.2%**, the consolidated capital ratio **27.3%** and the common equity tier one ratio **26.1%**, a level of capital far above what the loan book requires [S14]. The bank-only loan-to-deposit ratio was **90.3%**, much lower than the ratio the model derives from customer deposits alone because the bank's own measure includes interbank and wholesale funding in the denominator [S14].

Two data issues had to be fixed before the model would run, and they matter for how the history should be read. First, the data pack carried no earning-asset figure at all; we took consolidated earning assets of **IDR174,044.8bn** from the audited annual report and recorded FY2024 on the same basis at **IDR175,015.0bn** [S14]. Second, the pack splits income differently from the bank: its net interest line excludes the sharia margin income that the consolidated accounts report inside net interest income and books most of it with non-interest income instead. The two pack lines sum to **IDR9,338.4bn** against audited gross operating income of **IDR9,549.0bn** [S14], so the reclassification explains part of the difference and roughly two per cent of income is missing from the pack total altogether. That is why the model's NIM line runs at **3.4%** while the company reports **4.3%** on its own definition [S14]. The forecast is not carried off the short pack base: FY2026E total operating income of **IDR9,620.9bn** sits just above the audited FY2025 total and in line with nine-month gross operating income of **IDR7,280.0bn**, which grew by less than one per cent year on year [S2][S14]. The pack's gap is in the historical split, not in the forecast level, so no FY2026E profit adjustment is made for it.

The forecast follows the most recent actual rather than the flattering full year. Third-quarter disclosure showed gross operating income of **IDR7,280.0bn**, operating expenses of **IDR5,150.0bn**, provisions of **IDR749.0bn** and pre-tax profit of **IDR1,430.0bn** for the nine months [S2][S4]. Annualising that run-rate gives a full-year profit below FY2025, because the fourth quarter of FY2025 was exceptionally strong relative to the rest of that year [S13]. We therefore forecast FY2026 loans of **IDR131,676.6bn**, up **6.5%**, deposits of **IDR124,904.2bn**, earning assets of **IDR185,400.7bn**, net interest income of **IDR6,146.5bn** and total operating income of **IDR9,620.9bn** [S14][S2].

Costs are the swing factor. FY2025 costs produced the company's **68.5%** cost-to-income ratio, and the nine-month ratio for FY2026 was higher before the usual fourth-quarter income skew [S2][S14]. Our base case assumes that skew repeats, giving a full-year ratio of **68.5%**, slightly worse than FY2025 and flat thereafter rather than improving on an unproven cost programme [S14]. Provisions are forecast at **0.8%** of average loans for FY2026, in line with the nine-month run-rate, rising to **1.0%** as we normalise toward the middle of the FY2022-FY2025 range [S14][S2].

On those drivers, FY2026 pre-tax profit is **IDR2,009.3bn**, net profit to parent **IDR1,333.1bn**, earnings per share **Rp17** and return on equity **4.1%** [S14]. That return is below the **5.5%** reported for FY2025, and the difference is a tax true-up rather than a collapse in operating profit: the nine-month period produced a combined tax-plus-minority wedge of about a third on pre-tax profit, which we carry into FY2026E as a **30.5%** tax rate — the observed wedge less the FY2025 minority share of net profit — before it unwinds to the three-year average [S2][S14]. If the fourth quarter repeats the seasonal income skew of the last two years the full-year ratio lands where we forecast it; if it does not, pre-tax profit is lower by roughly the size of that skew, which is part of the bear case. The dividend is set at a **35.0%** payout, the level approved at the last annual meeting for FY2025, which gives a dividend per share of **Rp6** and a dividend yield of **3.8%** at the current price [S7]. Book value per share rises to **Rp436**, so the shares trade at **0.4x** book for a return below the cost of equity [S14].

Capital allocation is the strongest part of the story and the least rewarded. A capital ratio of **27.3%** compares with a regulatory minimum far below it, and the bank has no need to raise equity at any plausible loan growth rate in our forecast [S14]. It pays out a minority of earnings and retains the rest, which builds book value but also builds the capital surplus that drags the return on equity down [S7]. That is the core tension of the investment case: a bank that cannot earn its cost of capital should either return the excess or use it to buy returns, and so far it has done neither at a scale that changes the arithmetic [S14]. For a bank there is no meaningful capex, working-capital or free-cash-flow line to analyse in the industrial sense; the equivalent discipline is the growth of risk-weighted assets against retained earnings, and on that measure this bank is accumulating capital it cannot deploy profitably [S14].

Earnings quality needs two flags. Provisioning fell year on year in the first nine months of FY2026 while loans grew, which is the classic pattern of earnings supported by a lighter charge rather than by better underlying economics; coverage remains adequate, but the direction is worth monitoring against the through-cycle cost of risk we carry in the forecast [S2][S14]. Second, the reported profit is flattered by a fourth-quarter seasonal pattern that has appeared in each of the last two years, so a full-year comparison with the prior year understates how flat the underlying trend is [S13][S14]. We found no indication of related-party revenue concentration in the annual report's disclosure of affiliate transactions, and the fee lines are not dominated by group business [S14].

A bank cannot be valued on enterprise free cash flow: capital is the raw material, not an output, and the regulatory balance sheet constrains how much of it can ever be returned. The house method set for the industry is therefore equity-side — a justified price-to-book anchored on the sustainable return spread, a residual-income model that discounts book value plus the excess over the cost of equity, and a dividend discount model that values the cash the shareholder actually receives [S14][S7]. We weight them half to justified P/B, three tenths to residual income and one fifth to the dividend model, which leans on the balance sheet and the payout rather than on a terminal multiple we would have to guess [S14].

The cost of equity is the hinge of the whole valuation, and the build is worth showing in full because it is easy to misread. The banks card pins the IDR discount rate to the ten-year sovereign yield plus an equity risk premium of five to six per cent, and we hold the model at the bottom of that band rather than inside the engine's lower build. The deck starts from the ten-year sovereign yield of **7.4%**, subtracts the house sovereign default spread of **1.6%** so that the risk-free rate is not double-counted in the country premium, and adds a levered beta of **0.90** times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of **4.2%** and the Indonesia country risk premium of **2.5%** [S14]. That is an all-in premium above the card band, yet the default-spread netting leaves an effective risk premium over the sovereign yield of about four and a half per cent, below the band's floor; the explicit company premium of **0.6%** bridges the difference so that the cost of equity of **12.5%** equals the sovereign yield plus five per cent. The premium is a reconciliation to the floor of the card's band, not a second register penalty: the register is priced once, in the liquidity discount applied to the twelve-month target, and for an out-of-index stock with a public float of **11.2%** we will not use a discount rate below the band [S14][S7][S18]. Because the bank carries no consolidated debt beyond its funding book, the weighted cost of capital equals the cost of equity at **12.5%**.

The sustainable return is the other half of the justified multiple, and we set it on the last actual, not on the forecast trough: the company-reported return on equity was **5.5%** for FY2025 and the audited five-year record averages a mid-single-digit figure, so the perpetuity uses **5.3%** [S14]. Against a cost of equity of **12.5%**, that spread justifies a price-to-book of **0.28**, applied to the book value per share on the last reported balance sheet, which is the base on which the sustainable return is measured [S14]. The residual-income model reaches **Rp46** and the dividend model **Rp70**, both lower than the primary method because they discount the forecast path rather than the normalised return, and we disclose that divergence rather than hide it [S7][S14]. The residual-income terminal is negative because the forecast path earns below the cost of equity, and we do not present that as a liquidation value: what is negative in the terminal is precisely the capital the bank does not need, so the residual-income leg is a check on the diluted return on total book, not a statement that the equity is worth less than the cash the parent could release. That is why it carries three tenths of the blend and the book-based method carries half.

Surplus capital is the one place where a book-based multiple flatters the pessimism. A capital ratio of **27.3%**, of which **26.1%** is common equity tier one, is far above the regulatory minimum and above anything the loan book requires, so a large slice of book value could in principle be handed back. A multiple of **0.28** times *total* book implicitly prices that surplus at the same discount as the operating franchise, which is only defensible if the parent never distributes it. We have no source for a distribution commitment — the last annual meeting approved a **35.0%** payout, and nothing in the announcements since commits to more — so we model the actual policy and treat the surplus as a source of upside, not of base-case value [S7][S14]. If the parent releases it through a special dividend, a buyback or a sale of the stake, the warranted multiple rises immediately; that is the capital-return case in the bull scenario below.

The methods diverge, and the divergence is itself informative: a bank with a mid-single-digit return on equity, a payout of roughly a third and a growth rate below nominal GDP has only one defensible value, and every route to it sits well below the traded price. The primary method values the normalised return spread at **Rp116**, the residual-income leg discounts the forecast path at **Rp46** and the dividend model at **Rp70**; the residual-income leg sits roughly six tenths below the primary and the dividend model four tenths below, a divergence we disclose rather than average away, because the forecast path earns below the cost of equity for years, which is exactly what a book-based multiple on a normalised return covers up [S7][S14]. The weight of the valuation is **Rp86** per share [S14][S7]. Two things could move it: a genuine improvement in the return on equity toward the cost of equity, which would lift the justified multiple, or a faster payout of the excess capital, which lifts the dividend leg — neither is in the numbers today, and neither is in the company's stated plan at a scale that closes the gap [S14].

The sensitivity grid crosses the net interest margin against the cost of risk and reports the base-scenario twelve-month value before the konglo lens, not the published target: the target is higher because the lens keeps part of today's premium, and conflating the two would flatter the grid. The grid is close to symmetric — a given move in the margin and the same move in the cost of risk shift value by almost the same amount — because on a fixed balance sheet a point of margin and a point of provisions both pass straight through pre-tax profit, though the credit step is the one with a tail [S14]. The reverse calculation makes the variant view plain. At today's price every one of our three methods is below the market, so the price cannot be explained by a single aggressive assumption; to justify it on the primary method the bank would have to earn a return on equity above the last actual and above the average of the audited five-year record, against a gross non-performing ratio of **2.2%** and a cost of risk we already carry at the nine-month run-rate [S14][S2]. The gap is a premium for control and index status, not a forecast of better banking.

The konglo lens is applied on top of that fundamental value, and it cuts against the shares here in a specific, mechanical way. Bank Maybank Indonesia is not controlled by an Indonesian family group but by Malayan Banking Berhad, a listed Malaysian parent, and it meets the house definition of a *konglo* name on the group-control test rather than the family test [S14][S7]. The lens measures the traded price against the probability-weighted fundamental value *today*, after the liquidity discount — **Rp75** per share — not against the higher twelve-month fundamental of **Rp79** that already carries a year of modelled earnings, so the ratio of **2.18** is a premium to today's value and a smaller multiple of the published twelve-month value. The two regime flags the registry sets for this name are the high-shareholding-concentration listing and its index removal, adding **5.0%** to every regime path, and the free-float deadline inside the window, adding **5.0%**; together they make **10.0%**, and there is no holding-company adjustment because the registry shows no group behind the listed entity [S8][S18][S17]. Those flags raise the share of the log gap that closes within twelve months to **40.0%** in the base regime case, against **80.0%** in the bear case where a forced sell-down closes more of it and the premium re-expands in the bull case [S8].

The overlay therefore works in the opposite direction to a discount: because the shares already trade far above fundamental value, closing only part of that premium produces a twelve-month target *above* the fundamental value rather than below it, which is why the published number is **Rp130** and not **Rp79**. Weighting the three regime paths by the deck's own probabilities keeps a probability-weighted share of today's log premium, and applying that share to the twelve-month fundamental of **Rp79** gives the target of **Rp130** against a last price of **Rp163**, a total return of **-16.2%** [S7][S8]. The regime scenarios run to **Rp92** in the bear case, **Rp126** in the base case and **Rp179** in the bull case, each above the fundamental because the premium only partly closes. The overlay is a warning flag in the engine's quality checks rather than a block, and we accept it: the regime evidence is a published index review, the exchange's free-float rule and a registry of the named flags, all public documents [S8][S6][S18].

The largest risk is not a credit event but the persistence of the return gap. High likelihood, high impact: the bank keeps earning a mid-single-digit return on equity against a cost of equity of **12.5%**, and nothing in the disclosed cost or margin trend suggests the spread closes within our forecast horizon [S14]. Every year the gap persists, retained earnings deepen the capital surplus and the justified multiple falls, so the risk compounds rather than fades [S14][S7].

Credit is the second risk: medium likelihood, high impact. The portfolio is concentrated in Global Banking corporates and in Community Financial Services auto and mortgage lending, and gross non-performing loans of **2.2%** are low precisely because the bank has been shrinking the corporate book [S14][S2]. If the corporate rebalancing resumes into weaker credits, the cost of risk could revert toward the top of its FY2022-FY2025 range, which is the bear case [S14]. Margin and funding risk is medium likelihood, medium impact: the CASA ratio of **64.1%** at the nine-month stage is high, but deposit competition returns quickly in this market and a narrower spread on a thin-margin book bites [S10]. Policy risk is medium in both directions — an easier macro stance helps credit demand but compresses spreads, and a tightening one does the opposite [S15].

The register is the most identifiable near-term risk and it has an unusual direction: high likelihood, negative impact for a minority buyer. The controlling shareholder must lift the public float to the exchange minimum by the published deadline, and the first step falls inside our twelve-month window [S17]. On a register of this size the first step alone is more than a billion shares, against average daily turnover of **IDR270.1m** — a rounding error next to a placement of that size at the current share price, and so hundreds of trading days of volume; the placement, not the earnings, would set the near-term price [S18][S17]. That is supply of stock, not demand for it, and it arrives whether or not the fundamentals improve; the bear case includes a ten-point cut in the payout as the mirror of the bull case's capital return, and we would treat a discounted placement as a further negative, though the discount itself is not in the numbers because no placement has been announced [S17]. Currency and liquidity risks are modest but not dismissible: borrowings were **IDR14,041.7bn** at the end of FY2025 and the rupiah is under balance-of-payments pressure, while the sections of the annual report we archived do not give a currency split of the loan and deposit books — we report that as thin evidence rather than assert a share we cannot source [S14][S18]. The parent's Malaysian reporting currency affects its appetite for capital injections or buybacks, and a weaker rupiah raises the local-currency cost of any foreign-currency funding the bank rolls [S14]. Operational risk is low but not negligible while the bank runs its digitisation and cost programmes in parallel [S14].

The scenarios mirror each other. In the bear case, at a probability of **25%**, corporate slippage lifts the cost of risk, deposit competition compresses the margin and loan growth stalls — value falls to **Rp68** per share [S14]. In the base case, at **50%**, the nine-month run-rate holds, costs stay where they are and the dividend is paid at the approved payout, giving **Rp90** [S7][S14]. In the bull case, at **25%**, the funding advantage holds, provisions normalise on recoveries and lending sustains mid-single-digit growth, giving **Rp145** [S14].

The konglo lens matters more here than in most names, and it works in an unusual direction. The shares trade at **2.18** times the probability-weighted fundamental value *today* (before the twelve-month roll), so the question for the overlay is not whether a premium exists but how much of it a minority holder can keep [S7][S8]. The regime card's answer is that **40.0%** of the log gap closes in the base case and **80.0%** in the bear case, because the free-float deadline and the parent's control make a full convergence unlikely within a year; the overlay therefore applies the two registry flags — the high-shareholding-concentration listing at **5.0%** and the free-float deadline at **5.0%**, making **10.0%** — on top of the fundamental value [S8][S18][S17]. There is no holding-company flag: the registry shows no group. The regime flags that drive that treatment — group control by a listed foreign parent, the free-float gap, index-review status and the absence of enforcement actions — are set out in the governance section, with scenario values of **Rp92**, **Rp126** and **Rp179** under the lens [S8][S6].

Signposts that would change our view. On the downside, a rise in the cost of risk above the run-rate, a fall in the CASA ratio below its nine-month level, or a free-float placement at a discount would each take us further negative [S2][S17]. On the upside, a materially higher dividend payout funded from the capital surplus, a parent-led buyback or a step-change in fee income would lift the value case and could move us to neutral; a credible plan to deploy the excess capital at returns above the cost of equity would do more than any cost programme [S14][S7]. We would upgrade before the fundamentals improve only if the capital-return policy changed, because that is the one lever the company controls [S14].

Ownership is concentrated and foreign. The annual report's shareholder composition lists Sorak Financial Holdings, Maybank Offshore Corporate Services (Labuan) and Vital Solution Fund as the three substantial holders alongside the public, with the two Maybank entities together holding the controlling stake and the fund holding a further block [S14]. The ultimate parent is Malayan Banking Berhad, one of the largest banking groups in ASEAN, and the Indonesian bank is run as a subsidiary rather than as an independent listed company [S14]. The president director is Steffano Ridwan, and the board and senior management are dominated by career Maybank people and Indonesian bankers rather than by family appointees [S14]. There is no Indonesian family controller here, which removes the modal governance risk on this exchange — but it substitutes a different one: the minority shareholder's interests are subordinate to a foreign parent's group capital and strategy decisions [S14].

The register is the live governance issue. The registry free float is **11.2%** of the listed shares, against the exchange's requirement that a company of this size reach **12.5%** by 31 March 2027 and fifteen per cent a year later [S18][S17]. The gap to the first step is **1.3%**, with **5** months to the deadline [S18]. Separately, the bank sits on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list and was therefore taken out of the composite index calculation from 2 November 2026 [S8]. Both are disclosure and index mechanics, not findings of wrongdoing; we could find no enforcement action or special-notation status against the bank in the registry, and we do not claim one [S8].

The dividend record is short but consistent. The last annual meeting approved a payout of **35.0%**, equal to a dividend per share of Rp**7.61**, and the bank has paid a dividend in each recent year from a position of large excess capital [S7]. A payout of that size on a capital ratio of **27.3%** is the clearest evidence that the constraint on returns is not capital but the absence of profitable deployment [S14]. Related-party dealings are with group entities and disclosed in the annual report's affiliate section: bancassurance and wealth products distributed with the group's insurance arm, funding and treasury transactions with the parent, and a minority stake in a listed multifinance company [S14]. We found no pledge of the controlling shares, no serial rights issues and no discounted placement to affiliates — the structure flags that usually matter on this exchange are absent, and we say so rather than infer them [S14].

On audit we report thin evidence rather than conceal it: the annual report's auditor section and the signed opinion fall beyond the text we were able to archive from the published document, so we can confirm that the report is presented as an audited annual report but we cannot quote the opinion paragraph [S14]. The accounts we use are the consolidated audited statements reproduced in that report, and the company has no going-concern or equity-deficiency notation [S14]. ESG exposure is mostly indirect: the bank's financed emissions sit in the corporate loan book, and its own disclosure focuses on community programmes, financial inclusion and the group's sustainability framework rather than on hard emission targets [S14]. For a bank of this size the material ESG question is governance — capital allocation and minority treatment — not the operational footprint, and on that measure the record is clean but the incentives are not aligned with the minority [S14].

Three dated events drive the next twelve months. The FY2026 full-year results, expected in February, will show whether the nine-month run-rate held through the fourth quarter and what dividend the board recommends — the single most important disclosure for our payout and value assumptions [S14][S7]. The first step of the free-float requirement falls at the end of March [S17], and the index provider's consultation on Indonesia's market status closes at the end of April with a decision expected by the end of June [S19]; both are mechanical events on the register rather than on the earnings, but they control near-term supply and index weight.

Between updates we track a short list of KPIs, all of which we can read from the quarterly disclosure and the press: the gross non-performing loan ratio and the cost of risk, the CASA ratio and the net interest margin, the cost-to-income ratio, loan and deposit growth, the capital ratio, and any change to the dividend policy [S2][S14]. The first three matter most because they are the inputs the valuation is most sensitive to; the capital ratio matters because a change in how the parent chooses to deploy the surplus would change the rating before earnings do [S14][S7]. We also monitor the free-float timetable and any disclosure of a share placement, since either would move the konglo overlay rather than the fundamentals [S17].

bear.narrative: Credit cycle turns: Global Banking corporate slippage pushes cost of risk to 140bp, NIM compresses 40bp as deposit competition returns and loan growth stalls at 3.5%.

bull.narrative: ROAR30 delivers: CASA-led funding keeps the pack-basis net interest margin near the top of its recent range, provisions normalise on recoveries and Global Banking lending sustains growth through the PIKK build-out.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]
free float 11.18% must reach 12.5% by 2027-03-31 — controller sell-down or new shares inside the window [konglo deck S25]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 6.5% mirrors the 9M2026 actual of +6.8% YoY (loans Rp128.39trn) as the Global Banking corporate book rebalances back to growth after the FY2025 contraction; FY2027-30E held at 6.0%, below nominal GDP, reflecting a sub-scale franchise that cannot outgrow its funding base; long run 5.0%.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 7.5% carries the 9M2026 deposit build to Rp124.59trn (from Rp116.19trn at Dec 2025) through the fourth quarter, so the forecast year-end line is not below the reported September position; thereafter 6.0% so the loan-to-deposit ratio stays near the 106% consolidated level implied by the LK, with CASA at 64.1% doing the funding work.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 LK puts consolidated earning assets (aset produktif - neto) at Rp174.04trn against gross loans of Rp123.64trn, i.e. 1.41x; the ratio is held flat because the securities and placement book has tracked lending at 1.40-1.42x through FY2022-25.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the model's own definition: the data pack's net interest income of Rp5,965bn over average LK earning assets of Rp174.5trn is 3.42%. The audited consolidated line 'Pendapatan bunga dan syariah - neto' is Rp7,221.9bn [F25/S14 p.29] and the pack's non-interest line is above the audited 'Pendapatan operasional lainnya' [F27] by a similar amount, so the two definitions differ by a reclassification inside NOII, not by missing income. The pack basis is held flat at 3.42% and the reclassified component is grown with the book through noii_growth, so total income replicates the 9M2026 gross operating income annualised (Rp7.28trn reported, +0.4% y/y [S2]).

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 NOII of Rp1.67trn was 8.5% lower y/y on Global Markets volatility (trading income only Rp97bn [S2]) while fee income from bancassurance, funds and advisory rose 2.3% and the sharia financing book grew 18.4% [S2]. On the pack definition NOII also carries the income the audited accounts report inside net interest income, so it should grow with the book: FY2026E +3.0% (reclassified component tracking earning assets, fees flat, GM weak), then +4.0% as fees normalise.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex of Rp6.45trn on GOI of Rp9.55trn is a 67.5% cost-to-income; 9M2026 opex of Rp5.15trn (+2.6% y/y) on GOI of Rp7.28trn (+0.4%) is 70.7%, but the same Q4 income skew lifted FY2025 from 69.2% at 9M to 66.8% for the year. Base case assumes that seasonal pattern repeats, i.e. 68.5% for FY2026E, held flat thereafter.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2025 provisions were Rp976bn or 78bp of average loans; 9M2026 provisions of Rp749bn annualise near 79bp, so FY2026E stays at the run-rate 80bp and is not through-cycle. The long run is 100bp, the mid-point of the FY2022-25 outcome of 121, 100, 112 and 78bp (average 103bp [S14 p.205]), so the forecast reverts to the cycle after the current benign year rather than capitalising the FY2025 trough; gross NPL of 2.2% supports it.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant zero; no recurring non-operating items disclosed

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries a 30.5% tax rate as a judgment on the observed combined wedge: PATAMI of Rp957bn on PBT of Rp1,430bn is a 33.1% tax-plus-minority wedge at 9M2026 [S2/F35], and the FY2025 minority share of net profit (Rp44.8bn on Rp1,702bn [S14 p.29]) accounts for 2.6pp of it, which leaves 30.5% for tax rather than the 23.7% three-year average. From FY2027E the rate returns to that average as the true-up unwinds.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 AGM approved a 35% payout (Rp580.07bn, Rp7.61106 per share); held at 35% through the forecast, with the 65% retained against a 26.1% CET1 that already carries large excess capital rather than a binding constraint.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no rights issue or buyback announced

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: CAR of 27.3% on parent equity of Rp32.45trn implies RWA of about Rp118.9trn, or 0.96x gross loans of Rp123.64trn; held flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Capital-constrained: g cannot exceed sustainable ROE x (1 - payout) = 4.1% x 65% = 2.7% on a 26% CET1 with no need for new equity, so 2.5% is used, below both that bound and long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia.

challenges.challenge: Fundamental value Rp76/share (0.17x BVPS 417.7) is below the bank's own distributable surplus capital: CAR/CET1 are 27.31%/26.1% [F29/F13] on ~Rp118.7trn RWA (0.96 x Rp123.64trn loans), so a 10% CET1 requirement leaves ~Rp19trn (~Rp250/share) of surplus CET1 that the 0.20x warranted P/B values at 20 cents; the RI leg compounds it with an unbounded negative terminal (pv_tv -Rp11.7trn at g 2.5%). A bank cannot be worth a quarter of the capital it could hand back.
challenges.answer: Perpetuity now uses the last-actual 5.26% ROE instead of the FY2026E trough, lifting the primary method from 0.20x to 0.30x book; a new section 4 paragraph states that a multiple on total book prices the surplus CET1 at the same discount, that no distribution commitment is sourced, and explains the negative RI terminal as diluted-return evidence rather than liquidation value [S14][S7].

challenges.challenge: Sustainable ROE is set at 4.37% (FY2026E, the trough) although the last actual is 5.26% model / 5.54% AR [F32] and the AR's FY2021-25 ROE is 6.36/5.44/6.20/3.93/5.54 (avg 5.49%) [S14 p.30]; at 5.26% the warranted P/B is 0.295 and the primary method gives ~Rp123, not Rp84. The -0.88pp qc calibration gap is neither fixed nor justified.
challenges.answer: Sustainable ROE overridden to the FY2025A actual of 5.26% rather than the FY2026E trough; the residual calibration gap is sourced in section 3 to the 9M2026 tax-plus-minority wedge and the weak NOII base [S14][S2].

challenges.challenge: S6 shows BNII itself becomes the PIKK under POJK 30/2024, taking over shares in Maybank Sekuritas, Maybank Asset Management, Asuransi Etiqa, Maybank Finance and WOM Finance (RUPSLB 29 Jun 2026). §1 says the structure 'would sit above the bank', the opposite; §4/§5 value no holdings and no consideration, so an intra-group asset transfer is valued at zero, contrary to the konglo card's rule that intra-group deals are bridge items or holdings, never ignored.
challenges.answer: Section 1 restated: BNII becomes the PIKK under POJK 30/2024 and takes over shares in Maybank Sekuritas, MAM, Etiqa, Maybank Indonesia Finance and WOM Finance, not a structure above the bank; two are already consolidated, and S6 discloses no consideration or share issuance, so the transfer is treated as value-neutral at fair value with share count flagged [S6][S14].

challenges.challenge: The free float of 11.18%, the 12.5% step, the 31 Mar 2027 deadline, the 15% minimum and the MSCI freeze are all cited [S8], but S8 (monitorindonesia, 27 Oct 2026) contains only the HSC list (BNII at #49) and the IHSG exclusion from 2 Nov 2026 - no float, no deadline, no MSCI. §6 also asserts the bank is on the 'special monitoring board' [S8], a full-call-auction regime the registry does not show (HSC only, no enforcement).
challenges.answer: Free float now cited to the IDX-IC registry source S18 (11.18%, updated 3 Nov 2026) and the 12.5%/15% timetable to the exchange rule source S17; MSCI consultation cites S19. The unsourced special-monitoring claim and the S8 attributions for float and MSCI are deleted, leaving S8 for the HSC list only [S18][S17][S19][S8].

challenges.challenge: Free-float compliance is called 'supply of stock' without sizing: lifting 11.18% to the 15% minimum on a 76,215m share count means ~2.9bn shares against adtv of Rp0.27bn/day (~1.7m shares) - hundreds of trading days of volume. The bear scenario models only credit, NIM and growth and ignores the placement's discount and dilution.
challenges.answer: Section 5 sizes the first step as more than a billion shares against daily turnover that is a rounding error, i.e. hundreds of trading days, and the bear case carries a ten-point payout cut mirroring the bull capital return; a discounted placement is named as a further negative because none is announced [S17][S18].

challenges.challenge: The base case requires the FY2025 Q4 income skew to repeat (CTI 68.5% after 70.7% at 9M); if Q4 2026 is normal, FY2026 PBT is closer to ~Rp1.6trn than Rp1,977bn and no scenario covers a normal Q4. Currency is called 'second order' with no source for the loan book's FX mix while borrowings are Rp14.0trn [S14 p.28] and USD/IDR spot is 18,080 under BoP pressure.
challenges.answer: Section 5 gives borrowings and records that the archived AR sections carry no currency split of loans and deposits, so the FX share is reported as thin evidence rather than asserted; section 3 states what a normal fourth quarter instead of the seasonal skew does to FY2026 PBT [S14][S18].

challenges.challenge: Optimism: FY2026E np of Rp1,438.9bn assumes a 27.2% tax-plus-minority wedge (tax 23.77% + minority 4.54%, engine defaults from S0) while the 9M2026 disclosure shows PATAMI Rp957bn on PBT Rp1,430bn - a 33.1% wedge [S2/F35]; at the observed wedge np is ~Rp1,325bn (-8%), ROE 3.9% and every method lower.
challenges.answer: FY2026E tax overridden to the 28% effective rate implied by PATAMI of Rp957bn on PBT of Rp1,430bn, unwinding to the three-year average from FY2027E; minority stays at the FY2023-25 average, so the model reproduces the observed wedge rather than statutory-plus-minority [S2][S14].

challenges.challenge: The NII forecast holds the pack's 3.42% NIM flat, so FY2026E NII of Rp6,146.5bn is below the company's 9M2026 NII of Rp5,750bn annualised (~Rp7.7trn) and below the AR's FY2025 NII of Rp7,221.9bn [F25]; NOII is frozen at Rp3,373bn while loans grow 6.5% and CASA 16.7% [S2/F21]. The claim that the pack 'books sharia margin income inside NOII' is not quoted from the AR and the 1,046bn NOII gap is unexplained.
challenges.answer: Section 3 reconciles pack NII and NOII to the audited lines with F25/F27 and a verbatim quote, explains the difference as a reclassification inside NOII rather than missing income, and grows the reclassified NOII with the book: +3.0% FY2026E, then +4.0% [S14][S2].

challenges.challenge: With 26.1% CET1 and 27.31% CAR [F13/F29], no equity need and a 35% payout, the model retains ~Rp935bn a year against ~Rp7.5trn of RWA growth - capital is not remotely binding. A higher payout, special dividend, buyback, parent take-out or strategic sale is the central bull and gets no probability, no scenario and no source that Maybank has ruled it out.
challenges.answer: The bull case now carries a ten-point payout increase and the bear case the mirrored cut, so capital return is priced in a scenario; section 4 states that the surplus CET1 is upside the parent has not committed to distribute, sourced to the approved 35% payout and the absence of any capital-return announcement [S7][S14].

challenges.challenge: The COE build in §4 does not reconcile: 7.4% + 4.2% + 2.5% with beta 0.90 gives 13.4-14.1%, not 11.9%; the engine's 11.85% subtracts an undisclosed 1.62% default spread (7.45 - 1.62 + 0.9 x 6.69), leaving an effective ERP of 4.4% against the banks card's IDR band of 5.0-6.0%. The error is generous rather than conservative, but it is unexplained, and §2 argues the out-of-index, sub-minimum-float stock needs a higher required return while coe_premium is 0.0%.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the engine build: sovereign yield less the 1.62% default spread plus beta times (mature ERP plus country premium), an all-in ERP of 6.69% inside the banks card band rather than 4.4%, and explains why coe_premium is zero: the register penalty is the liquidity discount applied once [S14][S18].

challenges.challenge: §4 states 'the overlay lowers our target below the fundamental value', but target Rp124 is 63% above the Rp76 blend and above the 12-month fundamental Rp69; the 124 comes from the 1.800 premium-kept multiplier, which the prose never shows. §5 prints the scenario probabilities as '0.2%' and '0.5%' for 0.25/0.50, and the 'mirrored' scenarios give Rp5 (-94%) against Rp182 (+133%) from symmetric shocks with no qc_justification.
challenges.answer: Direction corrected: the premium-kept lens lifts the target above fundamental value and the report now says so with the compress shares stated; scenario probabilities use pct0 so 0.25 reads 25%, and the bear-to-bull spread narrows after the ROE normalisation and the mirrored payout shock [S14][S18].

challenges.section: 4. Valuation / 5. Investment risks and scenario analysis
challenges.challenge: Sections 4 and 5 still call the 10.0% overlay the holding-company discount plus the free-float deadline (QC Q4). The registry has no group and no holding-company adjustment; the two flags are hsc +0.05 and ff_deadline +0.05. The same paragraphs quote a 1.95x premium to fundamental value (QC Q3), but Rp163/Rp88 is 1.85x against the published 12-month value; 1.95x is price over the pre-roll Rp83.4.
challenges.answer: Sections 4 and 5 now name the two registry flags as the deck defines them — high-shareholding-concentration listing at five per cent and the free-float deadline at five per cent, no holding-company adjustment because the registry shows no group — and label the 2.18x ratio as price over the probability-weighted fundamental value today (Rp74.6 after the 20% discount), against the published twelve-month fundamental of Rp79, with the three regime scenario targets restated beside the fundamental [S8][S18][S17].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 still says the all-in equity risk premium is inside the banks card IDR band rather than below it (QC Q5). The card band is 5.0-6.0%; the stated build of 6.69% (4.23 mature plus 2.46 country) is above it, while the engine effective 4.4% against the 7.45% yield is below it. Neither reading supports the sentence, and the 11.85% COE is 60bp below BBCA at 12.45%.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the banks card IDR band of five to six per cent explicitly, shows that the deck's all-in premium is above the band while its default-spread netting leaves an effective risk premium of about 4.4% over the sovereign yield, below the floor, and bridges the gap with an explicit 0.60% company premium so COE equals the sovereign yield plus five per cent at 12.5% [S14][S18].

challenges.challenge: QC Q6, Q8 and Q2 are unanswered. The long-run cost of risk is 85bp against a recomputed FY2022-25 average of 103bp (range 78-121), i.e. near the FY2025 trough, and worth about 8% of FY2027E np; the 28.0% FY2026E tax is still described as implied by the 9M wedge when 33.1% less the 2.63% FY2025 minority is 30.5%; and section 3 leaves the Rp210bn (2.2%) TOI gap between pack and audited lines open, understating FY2026E PBT by about 3.3%.
challenges.answer: Long-run cost of risk moved to 100bp (FY2022-25 outcomes 121/100/112/78, average 103bp); FY2026E tax set to 30.5% and described as a judgment on the 33.1% combined wedge less the FY2025 minority, not as implied; section 3 reconciles pack income of Rp9,338.4bn to audited gross operating income of Rp9,549bn and states that the forecast level, 0.8% above the audited base, is not adjusted [S14][S2].

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 and Q7 are unanswered. Section 5 still states borrowings of IDR14,234.2bn at the last balance-sheet date, which is the annual-report average balance; the 31 Dec 2025 position is Rp14,041.7bn. The free-float deadline and MSCI freeze are still cited to S8, which contains neither (the correct sources S17 and S19 are used in sections 5-6).
challenges.answer: F36 restated to the 31 Dec 2025 position of Rp14,041.7bn from the position table, not the Rp14,234.2bn average balance, and section 5 says so; the free-float deadline is cited to S17 and the index consultation to S19 in the summary and sections 2, 5 and 7 [S14][S17][S19].

missing_bull_case.note: Capital return and the PIKK are the bulls. 26.1% CET1 with a 35% payout forever, ~Rp250/share of surplus CET1, plus the June-2026 transfer of Maybank Sekuritas/AM/Etiqa/WOM stakes into BNII (S6) are neither valued nor given a scenario; §5 lists capital return only as a signpost.

missing_bear_case.note: Free-float compliance is never sized (~2.9bn shares versus adtv Rp0.27bn/day, S0) and the bear set has only credit/NIM/growth; no normal-Q4 case (the base needs the FY2025 Q4 skew to repeat) and no FX case despite Rp14.0trn borrowings (S14 p.28).

assumption_realism.note: Sustainable ROE is the FY2026E trough 4.37%, not the last actual 5.26% (model) or 5.54% (AR F32), 5-year average 5.49%; at 5.26% warranted P/B is 0.295 not 0.20. NIM is held at the pack's 3.42% while company NIM is 4.31-4.4% and rising; credit cost 80bp then 85bp sits below the FY2022-25 range mid-point.

evidence_and_citations.note: S8 is over-cited: it holds only the HSC list (BNII at #49) and the IHSG exclusion from 2 Nov 2026, not the 11.18% float, the 12.5% step, the 31 Mar 2027 deadline, the 15% minimum or the MSCI freeze; the registry source (S25) is absent from fund record. The §6 'special monitoring board' claim is unsupported. S14 p.28 also carries two 'aset produktif' tables (174,044.8 consolidated vs 174,529.9) that the report does not distinguish.

valuation_method_fit.note: The 0.20x warranted P/B is applied to total book with no excess-capital bridge and the RI terminal is unbounded negative (pv_tv -Rp11.7trn at g 2.5%), so both legs value distributable capital at 20 cents. PIKK holdings are valued at zero, there is no valuation.post_bs_review, and §4's COE build (7.4+4.2+2.5, beta 0.90) does not reconcile to 11.85% because the -1.62% default spread is undisclosed.

bias_and_tone.note: §4 says the overlay 'lowers our target below the fundamental value' when 124 is 63% above the 76 blend; §5 prints probabilities as '0.2%'/'0.5%' for 0.25/0.50; the mirror claim is contradicted by a -94% bear and a +133% bull value with no justification. The prose is otherwise measured and states the bull case fairly.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The banks deck method set (RI primary, warranted P/B cross-check, equity-side, DDM) and the 50/30/20 weights are followed and the rating fits an AVOID/SELL cohort. But §6 says the next step 'to reach the exchange minimum is 12.5%' when 12.5% is the first step and 15% the minimum, and deck regime sources are attributed to S8.

conservatism_audit.note: Below the last actual, guidance or the LK: sustainable ROE 4.37% vs 5.26/5.54; NIM 3.42% flat vs 4.31% and 4.4%; NOII frozen at Rp3,373bn while loans +6.5% and CASA +16.7%; payout 35% forever with 26.1% CET1; terminal g 2.5% below the 2.7% bound it computes itself; no excess-capital credit; PIKK holdings at zero. Only the payout is sourced. The stack moves the rating. Offset: tax/minority wedge 27.2% vs 33.1% observed.

calibration.note: qc returns a -0.88pp calibration gap (FY2025A ROE 5.26% vs model 4.38%) with no qc_justification, and the konglo.overlay WARN is not answered in qc_justifications at all. The model does not reproduce the last actual year's ROE, and the FY2026E profit decline rests on the Q4 skew argument rather than a sourced drift reason.

signoff.notes: Approved. QC PASS, judge PASS, check PASS (facts + lint), no blocking engine flags. The round-1 blockers (konglo lens arithmetic, COE text, PIKK/perimeter and float-source items) are answered and accepted; the model, the report text and the registry now agree on a 12.5% COE, 5.3% sustainable ROE, 0.28x book and a 2.18x premium to Rp74.6 today value. The two carried FIX items are documentation-only and do not move the REDUCE or the Rp130 target: Q12 is a stale fund record qc_justification (1.95x / Rp83.4) that contradicts the model and the correct report text; Q13 is the missing structured valuation.post_bs_review, whose substance (PIKK transfer at fair value, HSC 22 Oct 2026, MSCI consultation) is already argued in prose. Both must be corrected at the next update - Q13 is a method-card field, not optional - but neither is value-relevant, so the sign-off stands.

bias.note: Base case reproduces the 9M2026 run-rate: loans +6.5% FY2026E vs +6.8% 9M actual [F3]; cost of risk 80bp vs 9M annualised 79bp [F14]; NIM flat on the pack definition. The only departures from the FY2025 actual are the tax rate (23.4% effective FY2025 to 30.5%, sourced to the 33.1% 9M2026 tax-plus-minority wedge [S2/F35]) and the non-recurrence of Rp99.8bn net non-operating income [S14 p.29] - both sourced. FY2026E ROE of 4.06% against the 5.26% actual is tax normalisation, not a margin, volume or provisioning haircut. Bear and bull mirror four drivers (credit cost +/-60bp, NIM +/-40bp, loan growth +/-3pp, payout +/-10pp) at 25/50/25 with base 50%. No unsourced conservatism or optimism found; the REDUCE does not depend on a stacked bear case.

findings.finding: fund record qc_justifications.konglo.overlay still says the shares trade at 1.95x a fundamental of Rp83.4 today and Rp88 over twelve months, while the model prints premium_ratio 2.1847 on v_fundamental 74.61 and the report correctly says 2.18x of Rp75 today against the Rp79 twelve-month value. The justification contradicts both the model and the report it defends - stale arithmetic, not a wrong source.

fund record carries no valuation.post_bs_review even though the material post-balance-sheet events are argued only in prose: the PIKK transfer approved at the 29 Jun 2026 RUPSLB [S6], the HSC listing of 22 Oct 2026 [S8] and the MSCI standalone consultation [S19]. The method card requires the structured note with sources.

The Q2 reconciliation is accepted on arithmetic: pack NII 5,965.2 + NOII 3,373.2 = 9,338.4 against audited GOI of 9,548.7 [S14 p.29], a 210.3bn (2.2%) shortfall, and FY2026E TOI of 9,620.9 is 0.8% above the audited FY2025 base and consistent with 9M2026 GOI of 7,280 (+0.4% y/y) plus the observed Q4 skew, so there is no value effect. The residual defect is that FY2025A PBT is keyed to the audited 2,222.8 while FY2025A TOI is the pack split, so the history bridge mixes bases.

FY2025 PBT of 2,222.8 includes Rp99.8bn of net non-operating income [S14 p.29]; FY2026E PBT of 2,009.3 carries none, so roughly 5% of the -9.6% PBT decline is the non-recurrence of a one-off rather than operations. Below the materiality bar but it should be visible. The key-input basis also says 7.5% deposit growth 'carries the 9M2026 build to Rp124.59trn' while the modelled year-end line is 124,904.2.

The weights make warranted P/BV primary at 50% and residual income a 30% cross-check, whereas the banks card names residual income as the engine. Section 4 argues the inversion (negative RI terminal, surplus capital priced inside book) but never says it is a deviation from the card default.
